title: Science Fiction's Big What If
objective: After this level you can explain how Jules Verne and H. G. Wells turned scientific what-ifs into fiction.
summary: Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) treated space travel as engineering; Wells's Time Machine (1895) used the future to look at class in his own society.

cards.headline: In 1865, a novel aimed a giant cannon at the Moon.
cards.body: In Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon, members of the Baltimore Gun Club build an enormous cannon to shoot a "space-bullet" to the Moon from Florida. Absurd? Partly. But it asks the question at the heart of science fiction, which deals with the impact of science, real or imagined, on people.

cards.headline: Verne asks: can it be done?
cards.body: Verne's novel was the first fiction to treat space travel as a coherent engineering problem, recognizing, for example, that there could be no air. Yet he found no plausible way to land his cannon-fired passengers. In the sequel, Round the Moon (1870), they whiz past the Moon, cataloging craters. Verne's what-if was about the machine: how would you actually get there?

cards.headline: Wells asks: what would it do to us?
cards.body: H. G. Wells studied biology under T. H. Huxley and became a science teacher, but his what-ifs pointed at society. In The Time Machine (1895), the Time Traveller reaches the year 802,701 and finds the gentle Eloi above ground and the Morlocks below, who prey on them. The Eloi stand for the leisure class, the Morlocks for the working class. In The War of the Worlds (1898), invading Martians are killed by Earth's bacteria.

questions.prompt: What was new about Verne's From the Earth to the Moon?

options.label: It landed its travelers safely on the Moon
It treated space travel as an engineering problem
It was the first story ever set on the Moon
options.rationale: Myths like Chang'e's are far older.

options.label: It warned about a class split in society

questions.explanation: Verne's novel was the first fiction to treat space travel as a coherent engineering problem, though he couldn't land his passengers.

questions.prompt: A new story imagines a pill that ends the need for sleep, then follows how it splits society into those who can afford it and those who can't. Whose kind of what-if is it closer to?

options.label: Verne's: how the pill would be engineered
options.rationale: The story is about society, not the machinery.

options.label: Neither: pills can't be science fiction
A fairy tale's: a wish granted by magic
options.rationale: The pill is imagined science, not magic.

options.label: Wells's: what the idea would do to society

questions.explanation: Like The Time Machine's Eloi and Morlocks, the story uses an imagined science to look at a society split by class: Wells's kind of what-if.

questions.prompt: In Level 8, Chang'e reached the Moon by swallowing an elixir of immortality. What sets Verne's Moon trip apart?

options.label: It is worked out as an engineering problem
His travelers fly to the Moon by magic
options.rationale: Verne fires them from a cannon.

options.label: His travelers become immortal on the Moon
It is told as a sacred story
options.rationale: Verne wrote a novel, not a myth.

questions.explanation: Myth sends Chang'e to the Moon by an elixir; Verne's novel treats the trip as engineering, down to there being no air.
